userStories.title: Follow any playback end to end, and see why the cluster needed more workers
userStories.description: An operator must be able to see exactly where a playback stalled and why the cluster needed more workers, not only that a film is transcoding. Metrics (JS-019) give totals: stalls happened, the queue is deep. This adds one OpenTelemetry trace per playback (PlaySessionId) across the api, stream and worker processes: PlaybackInfo and its decision with reasons; each segment request and where its time went (served from the store, waited on a job, started a job); the job queued, claimed (queue time, which worker) and its ffmpeg runs with their speed; helpers started, and helpers wanted but not started for lack of a free slot; and a failover (lock lost, reap, replacement). The reasons for more workers become metrics too, which autoscaling (JS-057) scales on, so the reason it scaled is visible. Viewers keep seeing in their app that a film is transcoding and why (JS-067).
acceptanceCriteria: One trace per playback session spans the api, stream and worker processes, its context carried in the transcode job row across the Postgres handoff

Given a stalled segment (over 5 s), its trace shows which part took the time: waiting for a free slot, an encode slower than real time, the upload, or reading the store; the stall metric links to the trace (exemplar)
A failover shows the dead worker's span end and the replacement's begin in one trace
Helper decisions are traced and counted: helpers started with the job's speed, and helpers wanted but not started because no slot was free

Demand for workers is a metric with its reason (jobs waiting for a slot and how long, helpers wanted but refused, jobs below real time), and the autoscaler's input is one of these, so why the cluster grew can be read back
Log lines carry the trace id (JS-022), so a trace leads to its logs
jellyfin-web's playback info still shows transcoding, its reasons and speed (JS-067), and stays right while helpers run (the viewer's own job may have ended)
Exported over OTLP to any backend, off by default; the dogfood runs a backend and the docs show reading a stall from it
Checked with real processes: a test collector receives a playback's trace from three processes, with a stall and a failover in it
userStories.notes: Needs a design review; the homelab has no tracing backend yet (Tempo suggested). Product owner (2026-11-08): wants to trace everything through the pipeline, see where something stalled and why more workers were needed; placed before P6 (Kubernetes). JS-024 review (UX): Sessions can show the viewer's job as done while helpers encode, and no log line says a helper started.

userStories.title: Use every GPU and CPU the cluster has
userStories.description: A worker uses whatever encoder hardware its node exposes (NVIDIA NVENC, Intel QSV or VAAPI, AMD VAAPI) and falls back to the CPU, so a cluster with GPUs uses them, as Jellyfin does on the dogfood's Intel iGPUs. fMP4 can't splice across encoder families (spikes/seam: x264 spliced with NVENC lost half the frames), so each stream is given the best family with room when it starts, and its helpers (JS-024) and failover stay in that family. A GPU can also serve a CPU-encoded stream by decoding for it, if its frames equal software decoding, so every node still helps every stream.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a family is chosen for a stream, helpers and failover within a family, and what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (playing on is the goal; a restart needs the product owner's decision); and whether a copy and a re-encode should share one slot pool (today a near-free copy holds a slot for the whole film like a multi-core re-encode); and whether a GPU family re-encodes above 1080 lines, from JS-148's figures (D-021)
A worker detects at start which encoders its node can run (a short test encode per family, not the ffmpeg build's list) and advertises them; a node with no GPU runs exactly as before
A new stream gets a GPU family when a worker of that family has a free slot, and the CPU otherwise; the encoder family stays in the spec hash and the decision is logged and metered with its reason
Helpers and failover of a GPU stream stay in its family; a seek, a restart and a helper's chunk splice cleanly on QSV/VAAPI and NVENC as the seam spike showed for one family
Hardware decoding for CPU-encoded streams only where its frames are measured equal to software decoding (per codec and family); otherwise software decoding

Tested on real hardware in its own tier chosen explicitly (never skipped): Intel QSV/VAAPI on the dogfood cluster's iGPUs and NVENC on a developer machine; jellyfin-web plays, seeks and recovers from a killed GPU worker
Operators see which encoder family and worker serve each stream (Sessions, metrics, JS-021 traces)
An optional GPU worker pool requests gpu.intel.com/i915 or nvidia.com/gpu through the vendor's device plugin ; a cluster without one runs CPU workers only; documented in docs/running.md
userStories.source: PRODUCT.md phase5-library; rewritten 2026-11-08: the product owner wants every GPU and CPU in the cluster used where possible, priority kept in P5
userStories.notes: The dogfood cluster has an Intel iGPU on each of its three nodes (gpu.intel.com/i915: 1 allocatable) and the user's Jellyfin requests one; the developer machine has an RTX 4070 Ti and an AMD iGPU. GPU tone mapping (libplacebo or vendor filters) gives frames unlike zscale's, so it splices only within its own family.

userStories.title: Kubernetes example manifests
userStories.description: Example manifests an operator applies with kubectl: deployments per role, readiness and liveness, Postgres (CNPG), configuration as plain files. Split from the Helm chart (JS-142) by the direction review, 2026-11-19: an operator cannot install jellyscale today.
acceptanceCriteria: Example manifests in the repository install jellyscale on a fresh cluster with kubectl alone (`kubectl apply -k` or `-f`), no Helm
Readiness and liveness probes per role

The manifests size CNPG's max_connections from their own configuration: every process's databaseMaxConns plus the direct connections each worker holds (liveness, lease keeper, and one per running scan, segment sweep or asset sweep pass), with headroom; configuration whose sum exceeds it is refused by a check
Each probe states what it depends on: liveness never depends on Postgres or a store, so a database failover restarts no pod; ffmpeg threads follow the pod's CPU limit, not the node's cores
The worker's liveness URL can come from the environment or a Secret, and the manifests never put a password in a process's arguments
docs/running.md says which Postgres connection modes are supported (session; a transaction-mode pooler or pgx exec mode, supported or not, by a check), and the manifests connect that way
A replica whose database stays broken leaves service, and the manifests' grace period and readiness lead match the documented ones
The example manifests declare trustedProxies for their ingress (D-020)

The procedure in docs/running.md for confirming declared proxies, followed against the example manifests' ingress, says what the operator sees and does when no address is counted (every answer 401, no refusal line), and no sentence there denies a log line the server writes (D-025, BL-221)
userStories.notes: JS-020 (2026-11-08): each worker holds one Postgres connection for its liveness lock, outside the pool, so a stock Postgres (max_connections 100) is exhausted at about 90 workers, long before its CPU (one primary carried 1600 streams on two cores' worth). Connections are the first wall when autoscaling. User (2026-11-08): plain manifests for kubectl are wanted beside the chart, not Helm only.

userStories.title: DOMAINS.md defines the domains; each domain's detail lives with it
userStories.description: DOMAINS.md is 141 KB, with single invariants thousands of words long on one line. Every agent reads it on every task, readers' tools cut its lines short, and it drifts from the code. It becomes the definition of the domains: for each domain its vocabulary, its boundary (what it owns and must not do), and its guarantees as numbered rules of one to three sentences. Each rule's full statement, rationale, measurements, tables, tests and history move whole to one file per domain under docs/domains/, read by tasks that touch that domain. Invariant numbers do not change. Documents and their checks only; no behaviour changes.
acceptanceCriteria: DOMAINS.md is organised by domain: each has its vocabulary, its boundary (owns, must not) and its rules; every invariant belongs to exactly one domain; the preamble says what the file is, that a rule and its section in the domain file bind together, and that a change which bends either updates both in the same change

Every invariant in DOMAINS.md is one to three sentences and at most 600 characters, keeps the number it has today (none renumbered or reused; a new rule takes the next number), and links to its section in its domain file
DOMAINS.md has no line over 600 characters and is under 40 KB in all; no domain file has a line over 1,000 characters
Each domain file under docs/domains/ has one section per rule, headed by the rule's number, holding its full statement, rationale, measurements, tables and the names of its tests
Nothing is lost: a check finds each old invariant's full text under its number in its domain file, and a check lists every old invariant's tests against the new files and fails when one is missing
No guarantee is weakened: a short rule contradicts nothing in its section, and any statement that says less than today's cites a decision id from tasks/decisions.json
Every existing citation still resolves, by a check that fails on a number with no rule: in code, docs/, ARCHITECTURE.md, tasks/prd.json and tasks/decisions.json

The regex-over-prose tests are removed or replaced by tests that compare a constant with the number the doc states; a check that reads a number or table from DOMAINS.md today (the lease table of 25, the window of 37) reads it from where it now lives and still fails when doc and code differ

The pointers change in the same change: CLAUDE.md, the role files in .claude/agents/ (the product owner's read list included) and the build workflow's instructions say every agent reads DOMAINS.md, and a task's agents also read the domain file of each domain the task touches

userStories.title: A user id in a request names the caller, or the request is refused
userStories.description: About twenty routes take a user id, in the path of the aliases jellyfin-web calls or in a userId query, and ignore it: the answer is the caller's data whatever the id says (routes.go:121, items.go:67). Nothing leaks, but an administrator who asks for another user's list is given their own under the other's name, and no test would notice a handler that started to honour the id without a check. Two handlers that do honour it carry two hand-written copies of the check, in two orders (sessions.go:346-372, user_configuration.go:160-175). This task makes one rule, in one place, before any handler runs.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first: compat/captures/user-scope-12.4.md and .json record, from a real Jellyfin 12.4 with an administrator and two non-administrators, for every route in compat/endpoints.yaml: the status, and whose data came back, when a non-administrator names the other non-administrator (in the path, and as userId in the query), names an id that is no user, names a malformed id, and when the administrator names a non-administrator. It also records what POST /Items/{itemId}/PlaybackInfo does with a UserId in its body and GET /Sessions with controllableByUserId

Route has Users: 'own' (the default) or 'admin-any'. 'admin-any' is exactly GET /Users/{userId}, POST /Users/Configuration, POST /Users/{userId}/Configuration and POST /UserItems/{itemId}/UserData. --print-routes writes user: for every route that is not 'anyone', and docs/access.md's table is held to it

One guard, before the handler: on every 'viewer' route, a user id in the {userId} path segment, the userId query, the controllableByUserId query or PlaybackInfo's body that is not the caller's answers 403 when the route is 'own', whoever asks, administrators included. Nothing is read or written for the other user. The caller's own id, dashed or compact, in any case, answers as with no id

On an 'admin-any' route one helper decides: a non-administrator naming another user gets 403 before any lookup, whether the id is a user or not; an administrator naming a user acts on that user; an administrator naming nobody known gets 404; a malformed id gets 400. sessions.go and user_configuration.go use the helper and hold no copy

TestAccess asks every 'viewer' route with viewer A's token and viewer B's id, in the path where the route has one and as userId in the query on every route: 403 on all of them. With the administrator's token and B's id: 403 on every 'own' route, and B's record on the four 'admin-any' routes. After the whole sweep B's rows in users, user_item_data, display_preferences and sessions are byte for byte what they were
An 'anyone' route ignores a user id: POST /Users/AuthenticateByName?userId={B} signs A in

Named mutants, each failing every run: the guard reads the path and not the query; the guard lets an administrator through on an 'own' route; the helper looks the user up before it refuses a non-administrator

The one case of JS-116's captured replay that changes is named in the pull request: a non-administrator naming an id that is no user on the Configuration routes got 404 as on Jellyfin and now gets 403, so that the answer no longer says whether the id is a user. Every other case passes unchanged
jellyfin-web still works: the e2e tier passes unchanged (it sends its own id everywhere), and the differential tier passes with no new entry, since its one user names itself

DOMAINS.md invariant 49 and the routes.go comment 'These act on the caller whatever userId says' say the new rule. docs/access.md lists, under 'Stricter than Jellyfin', that an administrator is served another user's view on four routes only, with the capture entry that shows Jellyfin serving it everywhere
userStories.notes: Changed answers, to list in the pull request: a request naming another user's id got 200 with the caller's data and now gets 403; the Configuration 404 above. Neither is visible to a viewer using a client, which always sends its own id.Tests make their second user by SQL, as user_configuration_integration_test.go does; no seeding route is added. Jellyfin's rule is RequestHelpers.GetUserId (Jellyfin.Api/Helpers/RequestHelpers.cs:67-81 at v12.4). Owner's decisions (2026-11-16, on Fable 5.2's access model, .results/access-model-fable-2026-11-16.md): pictures by id open to whoever holds the id, by name need a token; per-library access right after JS-033; a revoked or disabled user's running stream stops within 15 s; a viewer sees no other viewer's name; an administrator manages accounts but never browses, plays or reports as another user; a Policy field jellyscale does not enforce is refused when changed (400); 'may download' is honoured; operator keys are never users; no issue is filed on Findroid for now.

userStories.title: A re-encode's x264 preset is part of its spec, and its price follows the preset
userStories.description: Every x264 re-encode uses -preset veryfast (internal/transcode/ffmpeg.go, at both x264 sites). spikes/picture-quality measured faster at +2.5 VMAF on the mean and +3.5 to +5 on the worst frames for 1.2 to 1.6 times the CPU, and medium +0.5 more for 2.2 times. The owner decided (2026-11-19) that operators choose the preset, trading picture against the compute they pay for, with faster the default (JS-136). This task builds what that needs underneath: the spec carries the preset, so every worker that encodes a stream uses the same one (segments of two presets under one init segment fail in Chromium with PIPELINE_ERROR_DECODE, spikes/picture-quality), and Spec.Cost prices each preset from a film measured through a worker, so a worker admits as many jobs as it can keep at real time. The spike also found today's 0.8 cores for a 1080p job low for a hard film (1.36 CPU s per s at veryfast, pinned, unverified basis); this task measures it properly.
acceptanceCriteria: Spec has a preset, one of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow; it is part of Spec.Hash, so two specs that differ only in it have different hashes, and a spec stored before the field existed reads as veryfast and keeps its hash, so its stored segments are still served

The preset travels in the playlist and segment URLs as the spec's other fields do, so a request answered by any replica rebuilds the same spec and hash whatever that replica would choose; a test asks one stream's playlist and segments of two api replicas and finds one hash

A worker encodes with the spec's preset, never a setting of its own: a test reads the arguments of a re-encode and of an H.264 copy's fallback (recodeArgs) for two presets and finds each spec's preset in each; the HEVC and AV1 fallbacks keep their own presets and say so in docs/transcoding.md

In a rolling upgrade a worker from before this task never takes a job whose preset is not veryfast (it would encode veryfast under that spec's hash, which Chromium cannot decode after the init segment): a mixed-fleet test with a pinned release-before worker, as JS-030's, gives it a faster job and finds it made by a new worker, while veryfast jobs are still shared by both
A test with real segments: a store holding a stream's segments at one preset never serves them for a spec of another preset; the second spec's job encodes its own

A measurement test, run as the AV1 rows are, logs for each of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow, from a 1080p and a 4K real-film source, SDR and tone mapped, through a worker's own command, on Ubuntu 24.04's ffmpeg 6.1 and on ffmpeg 9: CPU seconds per second of film, and the time to the first segment and to the fourth on 2 and 4 CPUs; docs/transcoding.md records the figures with the machine and the command

Spec.Cost has a row per preset, SDR and tone mapped, 1080p and 4K, each at or above its measured figure with the margin docs/transcoding.md gives today; the HEVC fallback's x265Extra and the AV1 fallback's rows do not follow the x264 preset; if veryfast's rows are found low and raised, the pull request states, per row, viewers per worker before and after and what the next viewer on a full worker then sees, and the owner approves those numbers before it merges
With real processes: a worker given jobs whose costs add up to its cores, at faster and at medium, keeps each at 1.2 times real time or more without a helper
No viewer-visible change while every spec is veryfast: the transcode, seek and helper e2e scenarios pass as before
userStories.notes: Bump OutputVersion only if the arguments of a veryfast spec change; a spec read from before the field must keep its hash (invariant: stored segments of a spec are its output).

userStories.title: Operators choose the x264 preset, faster by default

acceptanceCriteria: A config key transcodePreset accepts superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow; left out it is faster; any other value stops the start of every role with an error naming the key and the accepted values

PlaybackInfo writes the configured preset into each new spec and its URLs; changing it and restarting gives new playbacks the new preset while a stream already playing keeps its spec's, and two api replicas configured differently each produce streams that play, because every later request carries the preset (JS-135)

docs/running.md gives, for each preset, the measured CPU against veryfast, the time to the first segment (JS-135's measurement) and the picture gain (VMAF from spikes/picture-quality), and says what changing it does to stored segments (new specs, the old swept as any unused spec)

A picture test on every tier, with ffmpeg's own psnr and ssim filters (CI's ffmpeg 6.1 has no libvmaf): a real-film clip encoded through the worker at faster, against its source under a 4 Mbps cap, has a higher PSNR-Y (the spike measured +0.27 to +0.92 dB) and a higher SSIM than at veryfast
The default change is listed under Changed guarantees: more CPU per viewer (fewer viewers per worker), up to about a second on a start on a full worker, a better picture

userStories.title: Each test that failed the merge queue on 2026-11-20 has a verdict from its log, and a named cause where a bounded reproduction finds one
userStories.description: Four merge-queue runs on 2026-11-20 failed on six internal/transcode integration tests, each on a PR that could not affect them (docs, plan, a CI action, a module bump), each passing on the next run. Whether any is a product race in a lease, a retry bound or a seek read is unverified. PRODUCT.md: failures are invisible; seeking and resuming just work. D-039. Reshaped by D-042: this task reads, measures within a box and briefs; the product owner's decision on its brief names the fix tasks. The TRUNCATE deadlock is JS-158.
acceptanceCriteria: The sightings are these seven, each named with its queue run: TestAWorkerForgottenWhileItLivesEndsItsExtractionAndItsLateRenewalMovesNoCutLeaseLater, TestAfterTheFileIsReplacedAMidFilmRunDrawsAndReadsByTheNewFilesTrack, TestACauseThatPersistsStartsAtMostThreeFreshJobsAndThenFails/the_source_store_cuts_a_read, TestWithTheTrackStoredASeekIntoALongCueReadsNoMoreOfTheFilmThanAnySeek/DVB, TestAJobThatStartsPastTheEndEndsDoneWithNoFFmpeg, BL-197's TestAnyReplicaServesAnySegmentAndOneJobStarts, and the e2e scenario that failed the queue that day

For every sighting, from its merge-queue log and before any reproduction, the record says what failed, and what a viewer would have seen had the same thing happened on a production cluster (nothing, a rebuffer, a wrong picture or subtitle, no film), or that the log cannot tell. BL-197's question is answered there: would a loaded production worker miss a heartbeat 0.7 s after a job starts and have the job restarted, or is that the test's short lease

Reproduction is bounded: under CI's shape (ffmpeg 6.1, 2 CPUs), at most 2 hours of wall-clock per sighting and 10 hours in all, the sightings whose log points at a lease, a retry bound or a seek read first; at least one attempt per sighting runs under load like the queue's (its shard beside it), not only the test alone. Runs, failures and minutes are recorded per sighting
Each sighting ends with one of three verdicts: product (cause named), test (cause named), or cause unknown. Not reproducing is never a verdict of test and never rules a product cause out

No fix lands in this task. Each named cause goes to the product owner in one brief, with what a viewer would have seen and the size of the fix; the decision names the fix tasks, each of which has a check that forces the named condition and fails before the fix
No retry wrapper, no skip, and no raised timeout anywhere, for a named cause or an unknown one

Recorded as a short table in docs/testing.md (sighting, queue run, runs and failures, verdict, cause, what a viewer would have seen); nothing checks the table's form by machine

userStories.title: No worker started by a transcode test outlives its test, so the next test's TRUNCATE never deadlocks with it
userStories.description: Two merge-queue runs on 2026-11-20 failed on a Postgres deadlock: a worker started by an earlier test was still recording a segment when the next test truncated the tables (read from the runs' logs by the lead). Each costs a merge-queue run of about an hour and delays the dogfood's redeploy. The cause as read is the tests'; whether the product can meet the same deadlock is not yet said. BL-178 is the same family (a kit's fresh() truncating under live workers). D-042.
acceptanceCriteria: The record in docs/testing.md names the two queue runs, the two statements that deadlocked, and which test's worker was still alive

It says whether anything in the product, not only a test, truncates or takes the same locks against a live worker; if so, what a viewer would have seen, and that comes back to the product owner as a brief before a product fix
A check forces the condition (a worker still recording a segment when the next test's tables are truncated) and fails before the fix, with real processes or real contention
After the fix, every worker a transcode integration test starts has stopped, and its last write has finished, before that test returns; the fix is at the cause in the test kit, not test by test
BL-178's fresh() is covered by the same fix, or the record says why it is a different cause and BL-178 stays open
No retry on deadlock, no skip, no raised timeout, and no product code changed to fit a test
No viewer-visible change
